newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil petroleum bill faces vote in Congress.
newsitem.headline: Brazil petroleum bill faces vote in Congress.

text.p: A committee in Brazil's Chamber of Deputies was due to meet and possibly vote later Tuesday on a bill regulating the opening of Brazil's petroleum industry to the private sector, congressional officials said.
But government-allied parties remained at odds over the contents of the legislation and the panel-level vote could be postponed or even cancelled altogether, they said.

The committee was due to meet at 1100 local/1400 GMT with the intention of voting on the bill. Government whips, impatient with its snail-paced progress, want to put the legislation to a full vote on the floor of the lower house later this week.

An aide to Deputy Eliseu Resende, who drew up the legislation, said the lawmaker was studying a last-minute proposal by the government that the bill be put directly to its full, lower-house vote, missing out the panel vote.
Such a manoeuver was allowed under congressional rules but would have to be approved by the panel, the aide said.
An aide to the government's chief whip in the Chamber of Deputies, Deputy Benito Gama, said there was still no agreement on several points of the bill.
"Of course, the aim is to hold the vote today but I don't know if (the government-allied parties) will reach an agreement in time," Gama's aide said.
He said the main bones of contention were:

-- an article in the bill obliging the government to keep control of state oil and gas giant Petrobras. The government-allied Liberal Front Party wants to remove that clause, allowing for a future privatization of Petrobras.

-- an article allowing private companies to import and export fuel under the auspices of by a National Energy Policy Council, a new government body to oversee the energy sector as a whole. Private companies argue they should not be subject to restrictions.

-- an article allowing fuel producers to sell directly to industrial consumers, including steelmakers, thermoelectric power stations and petrochemical plants. Private distributors already working in Brazil want to carry on acting as exclusive intermediaries.

-- an article allowing Petrobras to create subsidiaries or enter joint-ventures without seeking specific approval on each occasion from Congress. Left-wing parties say the clause is unconstitutional and have threatened to take court action if it is included in the bill.
